title: LOUISVILLE VILLAGE BOARD MEETS
full_story:
The Louisville Village Board met Thursday evening and took action on oiling and chipping of village streets, a variance for Salt and Strings Butchery, installing fencing around a water storage tank and updating the lease for Headstart.

Mayor Chris Rinehart called the meeting to order and then recognized visitors.  Ted Whitehead with Snedeker Risk Management briefly addressed the board and invited the mayor and trustees to the Hope Trust Annual Conference on July 23/24 at the Ameristar Resort in St. Charles, MO.  Whitehead also spoke of the village perhaps conducting joint training with Clay County Highway Engineer Darin Koelm for a couple of important topics.

Next, trustees approved the meeting agenda, past meeting minutes and the bills.  Mayor Rinehart then moved to discuss the fencing between village property and property of Nancy Byers.  The village has an agreement with Byers to maintain the fence and employees spend time each year replacing dilapidated fence boards.  Rinehart thought it would be better to install a fence that won’t require constant upkeep and offers some privacy.  He said a chain link fence with privacy panels might work best.  He pitched the idea to trustees for their input and discussion with two options offered, replacement of the old fence and the addition of a security fence around the ground water storage tank in the same general area.  The replacement fence alone carries a price tag of $18,950.  With the additional fence that includes locks and gates, the price climbs to $27,450.  The price quote was from Hodges Fence in Edgewood.  After several questions, a motion was made and seconded to approve the two-fence option using money from the village TIF funds.  The measure passed on a 5-1 vote with Scott Ikemire voting No.

At last week’s Special meeting, Mayor Rinehart floated the idea of creating a village ordinance to deal with the use of shipping containers as storage buildings within the village.  Rinehart said he did a search and came up with some sample ordinance language.  He asked for additional input from trustees.  Suggestions included limits on sizes like 10, 20 or 40 feet in length, specific colors, free of advertising, prohibited in front yards and only permitted the side and back of property and giving the mayor the discretion on approving applications.  Rinehart said he would bring back an ordinance proposal at a future meeting.

Last week’s meeting also included the topic of updating the Headstart lease for the K-1 Building.  Rinehart said Headstart uses three classrooms and other rooms at the building but would like to use another classroom that the village uses for document storage.  With some minor improvements such as painting and stripping and waxing floors to be made, on top of the additional classroom space, Trustees suggested raising the monthly lease fee from $2,200 to $2,500.  That measure passed unanimously.

Treasurer Kristina Hodges asked the board to approve her attendance for the IMTA (Illinois Municipal Treasurers Association) Annual Conference, June 7-9 in East Peoria, at a cost of $290.  Trustees approved her request.

Utilities Superintendent Troy Elwood stated that Salt and Strings Butchery is requesting a variance for the expansion of the back of their building along Vine St that might fall within village setback requirements.  It lead to a discussion about where measurements take place and what is stated in village ordinances.  Once trustees agreed on the language as it pertains to the village right of way, the motion was approved without dissent, which included a stipulation that Supt. Elwood ensures compliance with the approved variance.

Village Engineer Brandon Bridges presented information about the 2026 Oil and Chipping Program using MFT funds.  The map reveals the streets to be oil and chipped are in quadrant one of the village, primarily on the north side of Louisville.  It includes Barbee Ave., parts of Vandalia Rd., Pearl, Johnson, Garden, part of Vine, Madison, Bryant, Ova and Esco.  A few other streets are included in this year’s program, part of Tanner, Maxwell, Bailey, Moore, part of Steele and part of Erwin and Caroline Drive.  Trustees approved the measure unanimously at a cost of $44, 470.  While the cost is higher, it includes the use of a higher grade oil that includes polymers that can extend the life of roads where they are applied and allows for better sealing of the road surface.

The board then went into closed session and returned a short time later.  No action was taken when they returned to the open meeting and it was announced that Louisville will have Town-Wide Garage and Yard Sales on Saturday, June 13.  With all business complete, the meeting adjourned.

title: 6K FOR WATER TOMORROW
full_story:
The 2026 6k for Water will be held tomorrow for walkers and runners from all over Southern Illinois.  This is the 10th year for Flora’s 6k for Water where people come together to raise money for clean water.  703 million people worldwide lack access to clean water.

Flora’s 6k for Water partners with the Christian Humanitarian Organization, World Vision.  In the past 9 years, Flora has raised over $60,000 for efforts that dig wells, build rain catchments, teach hygiene and more through World Vision.

6 kilometers or 3.7 miles, is the average distance that women and children all over the world walk daily for water.  As a result, children do not get the chance to go to school, they have the fear of being kidnapped and being trafficked.  Clean water within a village equals freedom from those things.  Nearly 800 children die each day from water-related illnesses.  You can help bring clean water to these communities.  World Vision reaches a new person with clean water every 10 seconds.

The race begins at 9 AM at the Flora First Christian Church.  No need to attend FCC to join.  This is a community event.

Each registration equals clean water for 1 person for the rest of their life.

The Flora 6k for Water will be held tomorrow morning at 9 AM at the Flora First Christian Church.

title: FLORA CLEAN-UP DAYS
full_story:
The City of Flora will have town-wide clean-up days Monday through the Friday.

Accumulated, unwanted items at residences will be picked up at no extra charge on the residents normal trash day.  It is requested small or loose items should be bundled or bagged.  Carpet needs to be cut and tied so one person can handle it, broken glass items need to be bagged and marked for safety, multiple items such as brooms, mops, blinds, etc. need to be tied together, pool liners need to be cut down, and metal swing sets need to be broken down.  All mattresses and box springs must be wrapped in plastic, in order to be picked up.

For electronic items such as televisions and monitors, radios, tape recorders, computer hard drives, monitors, printers, cell phones, etc. residents are ask to please contact Secure Processors at 618-662-4823.

Republic Services, Flora’s solid waste hauler, will not accept any white goods such as stoves, dishwashers, washing machines, clothes dryers, etc., tires or vehicle/boat parts, paint, hazardous materials/waste, landscape waste, construction/remodeling/demolition materials, concrete/brick/asphalt, batteries, pressurized tanks, gas/oil/antifreeze, ammunition, or explosives.

Residents may deliver their properly decommissioned, no Freon or Oil, white goods to Public Works West lot at 200 Fairview Street.  Please follow the signs posted.  This will be a residential only pick up site.  The city will only be accepting white goods daily between the hours of 7:30 am to 3:30 pm.

Please keep weight in mind when grouping items, such as books and magazines, in a bag or trash container.

Residents with any further questions should call 618-662-4625 or email [email protected].

title: OREP RESULTS
full_story:
Illinois State Police (ISP) Troop 9 Commander, Lieutenant Bruce Waggoner, announces the results of Occupant Restraint Enforcement Patrols (OREP) held in Clay and Wayne counties during April.  These OREPs provided extra patrol coverage for the ISP so officers could focus on saving lives by making sure all vehicle occupants were buckled up.

Troopers wrote 29 safety belt citations, 2 child restraint citations; 35 total citations and 7 written warnings.

Most motorists know safety belts save lives, but some ignore their safety and that of their families by neglecting to use safety belts and child restraint devices.  These patrols reinforce the occupant protection message by focusing on those who ignore the law.  Lives can be saved if people simply “buckle up!”  This project was funded through the Illinois Department of Transportation.

title: IDPH WARNS OF PESTS
full_story:
With warmer weather on the horizon, the Illinois Department of Health is urging people to take precautions against illnesses spread by animals and pests.

The IDPH said there are certain steps and actions people can take to reduce their risk of contracting any serious illnesses.

“Spring and summer provide so many opportunities for outdoor fun all across Illinois,” said IDPH Director Dr. Sameer Vohra.  “It is important to remember that some common biting pests and animals may be carrying disease that can cause serious human illnesses.  Illinois residents should take precautions like wearing bug repellent and vaccinating their pets against rabies, among other measures, to keep themselves and their communities healthy and safe.”

The first mosquito batches that tested positive for West Nile Virus in Illinois in 2026 were found in Cook County.  While no human cases have been reported so far this year, in 2025 there were 150 human cases and 10 deaths across the state.

This virus is transmitted through the bite of a Culex mosquito, also known as a house mosquito, that has picked up the virus by feeding on an infected bird.  Symptoms of West Nile include fever, nausea, headache and muscle aches but most people infected won’t show any symptoms.  The IDPH urges people to combat the virus through the 3 R’s – reduce, repel and report.

The IDPH said ticks can spread a number of serious illnesses, including Lyme disease, spotted fever group rickettsiosis, ehrlichiosis and others.  They said the best protective measure against tickborne illness is preventing tick bites.  Some tips to avoid tick bites include, walk in the center of trails, wear light-colored clothing to make ticks easier to find, tuck long pants into socks and boots, conduct full-body tick checks on family members every two or three hours, to kill ticks after being outdoors, put clothes in the dryer on high for 10 minutes, Bathe or shower within two hours after coming indoors.

IDPH also tracks cases of rabies in animals.  This disease is most commonly found in bats, and so far in 2026, two bats have tested positive for rabies; one of those bats was found in Sangamon County.

The greatest risk of exposure comes from bats that make their way into people’s homes.  If this happens to you, health officials suggest covering the bat with a container and contacting animal control so it can be tested.

title: ILLINOIS CONGRESSIONAL MAP SUIT
full_story:
Illinois’ congressional district map is being challenged over what some argue are unconstitutional racial requirements for districts.  A former Republican state representative sued Governor J.B. Pritzker and the State Board of Elections late last week.

Jeanne Ives, a former representative of the state’s 42nd district, brought the case backed by J. Christian Adams, president and general counsel of the Public Interest Legal Foundation.

Filed in the US District Court in the Central District of Illinois, the official complaint claims congressional maps drawn after the 2020 US Census are unconstitutional because the Illinois Voting Rights Act of 2011 mandates the creation of “racial districts.”

Ives told The Center Square Daily that state Democrats have brazenly moved to draw maps based on racial lines.

“It’s very obvious to anybody looking at Illinois maps, and Illinois law, that these districts are in fact, they use race to design the districts and the SCOTUS decision makes it abundantly clear that you just can’t do that anymore,” Ives said.

Ives said a recent US Supreme Court ruling, which determined Louisiana’s district map as unconstitutional because of an over-reliance on race, is what has explicitly made it clear that Illinois’ congressional map as unconstitutional.

“Pritzker went into 2018 promising an independent commission to draw the maps.  He comes out of the 2020 census with the most partisan map drawing that literally split precincts,” Ives said.

Adams, serving as legal counsel on the lawsuit, told The Center Square Daily that the goal of their legal challenge is not to remove race entirely from the map drawing process.

“The remedy is to not have explicit racial redistricting criteria.  You know, you can still draw districts in the country that have racial outcomes,” Adams said.  “Racial districts aren’t per se illegal.  What is illegal is having state redistricting criteria that is established ahead of time that says you have to create these racial districts.”

Last year, Republican state lawmakers challenged Illinois’ state legislative map as heavily gerrymandered.  The Illinois Supreme Court ultimately dismissed the case on the grounds of timeliness, rather than ruling on whether the map was lawful.

In response to the Louisiana ruling, Illinois State Senate leadership also killed an attempt to amend the state Constitution, which would have further enshrined a requirement for minority-representative districts.

Adams said that Illinois is the first state he is looking to challenge due to the nature of the maps.

Due to procedural rules, the Board of Elections and Pritzker have three weeks from the filing date to respond to the lawsuit’s claims.  Adams said a hearing on the lawsuit will not take place until at least next month.
